| [LIT-049](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-049.md) v2 | A coarse-graining account of individuality: how the emergence of individuals represents a summary of lower-level evolutionary processes | Bourrat (2023), DOI-10.1007/s10539-023-09917-x. Bourrat proposes that a partition of particles into collectives defines individuals when the "projected" prediction (coarse-grain at t1, then evolve the coarse-grained state) differs from the "truthful" one (evolve at the fine grain, then coarse-grain at t2) by δC = C_T − C_P < θ, across many traits (Eqs. 1–2). He argues that, because measurement and computation are finite, coarse-graining can be the only way to predict at all: in his example, 100 operations predict 10 entities for 10 timesteps or 2 collectives for 50. That indispensability is his whole case for the "quasi-ontological" status of collectives at Godfrey-Smith and Kerr's fifth stage. Nothing is computed on any model. | Proposed — read in full 2026-09-25 ([NOTE-064](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-064.md)); a lucid philosophical statement of "individual = a coarse-graining worth its cost". Its formal criterion is informal and, as written, degenerate: minimal δC picks the finest partition, and the cost term the argument depends on is never put into the criterion.
